claims.text: Adding Zr to a high-entropy alloy can improve its hardness.
Adding Zr to a high-entropy alloy can improve its strength without sacrificing useful mechanical performance.
The target alloy is initially in an as-cast state.
The intervention is addition of Zr to the alloy composition.
The hypothesized effect should hold when the alloy undergoes thermomechanical treatment, including hot rolling and annealing.
Zr has a large atomic radius and can produce solid-solution strengthening.
The Zr-induced grain-size and grain-boundary changes improve mechanical properties.
Relative to an alloy without Zr, Zr addition improves yield strength.
Relative to an alloy without Zr, Zr addition improves ductility.
The benefits depend on an optimal Zr content and suitable thermomechanical treatment route.
A series varying Zr content and thermomechanical treatment can test effects on yield strength, ductility, grain size, and grain-boundary refinement.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator attributes strengthening to solid-solution effects from atomic-size mismatch, whereas the mechanism switches to increased grain size and grain-boundary refinement without connecting those changes to solid-solution strengthening.

The simultaneous claims of increased grain size and grain-boundary refinement are ambiguous and potentially opposed, because grain-boundary refinement ordinarily implies a finer-grained microstructure.
Zr addition is presented as the single intervention, but thermomechanical treatment routes are also varied, making the effect of Zr alone potentially confounded.
